The Reformation Motto was painted on one of the kitchen cupboards, though Rinna guessed that Mama was the one who said that in the house. She didn't know when her father had written it down; everything had a place in one of the lesson notebooks he'd kept. She hadn't found all of them yet, but as soon as she'd opened the one downstairs beside the piano, the first thing she thought of was how Mama-Mimsie to everyone, but known to Rinna as Mama-must have felt when he'd written on the inscription page, Catherine's daughter. Mimsie worked all night?

Sometimes, on summer mornings Rinna would pound her shoes on the lower steps to wake everybody up. Today she paused halfway down to wonder if Mimsie laughed all night. She always wore a smile, and had clear dark eyes behind the tasteful frames on her nose. She looked like a young dietitian. She'd started working on this project herself, she'd told him, because it would be good for the environment and the people. Two, something like that, she said.

We always been fair, Pete said. You been fair as long as I've been around. Why's that not fair?

Pete, Marty said. You ever see those TV shows where they give families a new house for free?

It was fifty degrees outside by seven; the forecast was for even milder temperatures, and the president had canceled his rally for Tuesday.

Elizabeth sat on a folding chair in front of the silent building, wondering how many people it would take storming in at once to overpower the guards. How strange the building would sound after civilians took it over: chatter in the corridors, loudspeakers paging employees.

Now after decades of conscious and subconscious startups aimed at building community, moving multiple people at one time, with hugely successful companies like Uber, Lyft and Postmates, all vying to be the best in their respective race, we find fewer and fewer people actually using them. It's midnight in his body and noon in his head and all the corn is piled in a head-high wall in every direction. It's August and a very dense cornfield that happens to have a layer of razor wire on top of it and the cows were here two days ago, poking their heads through and setting off the alarm, and fence somebody else lassoed.

And Nick maybe has a little cocaine (telling no lies) or has maybe tried it a few times in the last year, he's not that much of a square. 

The wind is steady from the west and not strong enough to ruffle corn stalks or lap at their fringes. Nobody in the corn has a drink in his or her hands. When the scare begins people unhook their buckets and move through the tall plants as best they can toward the patrol wagon, which has pulled up with its lights on. Some are friendly enough to take my elbow or my outstretched hand. Some youngster with an athletic wire gauge runs a second ahead so I won’t fall with the volume of human traffic shifting between the almost invisible ground. 

Nick and I sit facing each other near the front, our knees touching. I think, “every night I have a drink and sit with a friend for company,” and then I think, “why am I burning out the things that give me such brief pleasures at all costs.”

Jay MacCleave sat at the other register, his elbows on the panel and his version of a computer to the side. Oddly, there was more red plastic than metal or steel: red plastic wheels, red and chrome grilling, and a red metal butt against a red plastic casing. Marty walked across the diner parking lot to the senior apartments and honked the horn.

On the north side of the square several residents came over, dressed for the unseasonable heat. They said they'd never ridden the bus. Marty could tell they hadn't. They were cheerful, engaged citizens uptil 4 pm when their phones started ringing. You would have thought his business was shutting down instead of thriving, the way they cried and complained.

They begged him to keep driving. He tried to be honest, he told them why he couldn't. They wouldn't have it. One man mobilized the retirees on Facebook. Another got an inland representative to vouch for him. Meanwhile, the phone calls and messages just escalated.

By the end of the week Marty had put together a petition with almost two thousand signatures and presented it to the city council. People cheered when the council passed a resolution in Marty's favor and told him to keep driving. He couldn't bear to tell them where the council was getting the money—not only the cost of the bus, but new funding (new taxes) for the drivers' salaries and benefits.

The next day Route 9 arrived on schedule. On cue, as he happened by, Marty honked the horn. The bus driver looked disturbed, and not in a way that could be written off as guilt. What was he up to?

Marty drove that afternoon, his first shift in weeks. The phone in the kitchen rang steadily. Pete didn't answer it. The porch light stayed off as though nobody was home, and Marty let it. One call at a time composed itself on the answering machine.

A pension the right way—Social Security or annuities—requires a forty-five-year commitment. Nothing in this world is worth forty-five years of your life.

Marty scrolled down to the detailed report. A complete breakdown was listed by date, along with the day's total. There was no way to tell whether yesterday's number had pushed them below or above nine thousand.

He sipped his coffee and saw Ray Pokorny turn onto the street and slow. Ray hadn't worked in a proper job for fifteen years, getting by in a world of minor deals and a lot of hope. Now he drove Route 9 mornings for the agency, Ray's wide smile going from passenger to passenger across the flat plexiglass window.

Marty gestured to the curb, and Ray pulled in front of him and turned off the bus's engine. Neither driver rolled down his window all the way. They regarded each other over the gap.

"Where are they going to run it now?" Ray asked.

"Around here, I guess," Marty said. "What time's your shift over?"

"Two. Why?"

Marty nodded at the time on his phone. "Come have some coffee in an hour."

Ray shook his head. "I do that, Bettsy'll wonder where I went."

They smiled uneasily at each other, the gap between them as wide as ever.

Marty saw no brake lights go on as she accelerated.

He braked hard, ducking through the stop sign, but he clipped her rear bumper, his own front bumper crumpling up. The skin on his right arm was scraped and bleeding. Mrs. Kirshner's head twisted at the impact.

The woman stared at him through her rearview mirror. "What the hell?"

Mrs. Kirshner scolded Marty. "Can't you watch the road?"

His own anger was beginning to vibrate his voice. He was still holding his battered arm. "That woman sped up."

Marty turned his cab in and got the contact information from the woman. He asked if she had insurance. She gave him a card. Her address was in Millport, on the north side. He called his insurance company, expecting the loss of his only cab to cost him half his livelihood: eighteen hundred a month.

He waited for two days for a call from the claims adjuster. When it came, Marty had to interrupt a conversation with Mrs. Kirshner.

averaged ninety-seven and a half rides a day, the paper said.

(Marty did the math: Ninety-seven and a half, that would be nine thousand six hundred forty-five. He opened the news story. It said "The results of the trial will be reviewed by County Council at their meeting Tuesday night.")

Marty finished his coffee and closed the page. He heard his phone ring, and let it ring on.

He looked out the window. A young woman in bright orange rain boots sprinted across the street. She wore light-grey sweatpants, a heavy raincoat, and a knockoff Yankees baseball cap pulled down below her eyes. She had dark hair hanging loose on both sides, halfway past her shoulders, and big dark glasses that made her look startled. She stopped at the curb and leaned over, hands on her knees, then took out her phone and checked the street.

Marty's phone rang again. He didn't answer.

The woman scanned the street and came back to the curb. She checked her phone again and at the same moment a big yellow-green AAR Transit Corporation bus pulled up. She glanced inside the window, then stepped up and on before Marty could open his door and call her back.

She wasn't holding anything. She tossed her phone onto the seat beside her, pulled the subway measure from her pocket, unfolded it and started tapping her thumb on the folded metal tab at the end. The bus pulled away.

(Marty could just barely see her now, outlined against the back window. Every time she tapped, the safety bar dipped by about half an inch.)

Marty's phone rang a third time. He let it ring. He clicked her phone number and looked at the call screen.

(Called ID: 5/8/21)

He closed the screen. The phone number lit up in his mind.

(Marty didn't think it was a problem, but he'd never gotten over it. He tried to believe that as long as he answered questions and let people have whatever they were entitled to, it was okay. It was okay even if he didn't like what they were entitled to, if they were rude or unlucky or wrong. It was okay if the problems they caused were worse than if he just said no.)

"Yessiree Bob," said Marty. "It sure is great to be back on the road again."

Marty Sobczak had owned Millport Cab for twenty-six years: two cars, himself and his nephew Pete driving, and a game room in the back where Pete's wife, Lydia, watched children while she waited for him to finish his shift. Most of Marty's fares were older folks who didn't drive anymore, going to the grocery store or the clinic or physical therapy. Millport Cab was a good, old-fashioned taxi: scratchy black vinyl seats, a divider that didn't close all the way, and in each back seat, a red crew sock.

In January, the regional transit agency started a three-month trial of a new bus route: Route 9, a loop from the senior apartments and the other side of town to the grocery store, the clinic, the library and the community college every forty minutes. At first Marty's fares were down by a third. To justify the bus route, the agency said, it had to average a hundred rides a day, every day, over the trial length: nine thousand by the end of March. If it fell short, the money would go to a route in another county.

Marty wouldn't have cared if the route stayed or not. He was sixty-one and had no pension. If the route stayed, he'd have to sell one of his red cars and Pete, who had a baby on the way, would be out of a job. Marty didn't think the town needed a bus that ran half-empty at taxpayer expense. He'd said so at a council meeting, politely. The local paper had followed the numbers all winter. Route 9 averaged 100 rides a day. Every. Single. Day. For three months. Nobody at the agency would guess how it would come out.

On Monday morning in March, Marty sat in the cab outside the diner with his coffee and opened the agency's website on his cell phone, bubbling over with excitement. The final numbers were posted at the top of the page: the Route 9 trial had averaged 100 rides a day for the full length of the trial.

Marty wished Pete good luck on the new baby.

He heard Pete's girlfriend crying in the background. "It's all right, honey," Pete said into the phone. "Just a tough morning. No need to cry over spilled milk. I'll come by after I talk to Marty." He paused. "Yeah. Well, I guess we'll hang on a while longer."

Marty took the next left and drove toward the highway out of town. There was no one in the cab except him, and he turned the radio high.

He looked down at the phone's screen. A new email had just arrived. He touched the icon. The local transit agency needed a driver for another cab. Marty usually drove the same route every day, and knew it well enough to drive it with his eyes closed. Drivers rescued the agency a few times each winter by filling in sick or on vacation for whoever had seniority.

Marty double-tapped the email and brought up the details. The rate was the same as what he made now, but they'd pay a ten-dollar sign-on bonus for the inconvenience of switching the route he knew. The new cab picked up at all hours of the night, days, and weekends. "We understand this isn't ideal," the email said. "But it's what's available, and we appreciate your willingness to help us out in a pinch." Marty had been a pinch driver himself, back in the early days.

He shut off the radio and steered back into the main street. It was only a little after eight, too early to call Pete with the news. Peel Street was shiny in the spring morning, and Marty looked at the shops that he'd been taking passengers to for twenty-six years.

All winter he'd wondered how the numbers would come out, and now that he knew, he didn't feel much one way or the other. He let the cab idle and sat still for a while, listening to birds and the distant music from a shop's open door.

Finally he replied to the email, telling them he couldn't take the job. Then he rang off work for the day and drove the long way home.

'Hello, Mrs. Franks?'

'Tomorrow and Wednesday, while I get things sorted out,' he said.

Her voice sounded faraway. 'That's fine, Marty,' she said.

He hung up, finished his coffee, opened the door, and looked out at the street. It was a chilly day, and the town was already quiet for lunchtime. No customers in sight.

He took a breath, climbs out and begin walking down the street, his hands in his coat pockets. The air was damp and smelled like dry leaves and gas station oil. He might not be able to keep the Porsche, but he and Pete could keep working, and Mrs. Franks wouldn't be alone as often. Her grandsons were good boys, but they weren't getting any younger. Sometimes Marty wondered what would happen to her if something happened to them.

The sun came out while Marty walked. The town didn't look so bad.

Every few steps a car rolled by. Sometimes the driver waved, and Marty waved back. He liked being outdoors and wished he did it more often.

When he looked at it, it was cracked, but it still worked after he wiped it off and stuck the pieces back together with electrical tape. They watched the bus take their place in front of the clinic the next morning. It was one of those new, low-floor buses, no steps, and it pulled up with a hiss. Half the people who'd used to give Marty a wave just wandered up to it and got on, their bags in hand like they'd been waiting to board all their lives. Marty was in the kitchen making toast for the baby—the shape of a peanut, his wife said, with a head like a cauliflower—and he watched them through the window while he listened to the engine idle.

In the first cab, Hardin was slowing for a red light directly across from the cab in the next lane. At that moment Marty got a text.

It said only: "Cut brake line."

He looked up and saw Hardin's rear wheels lock and the car in front of him skid forward as the cab lurched forward on the greasy light. In the cab across, the driver's head snapped forward and the horn blared. Marty's cab was still at the light, inches back, protected by Hardin's car, but now everyone behind Hardin was stuck. Tires screeched, horns blared, and then suddenly Hardin's cab was rolling forward again, past the light, past the intersection, past the cars waiting to turn, going faster and faster with no brake lights on and the horn still blaring. The traffic light cycled and Hardin blew through the next two intersections, past the courthouse and the post office, horn blaring. Marty ran his light and followed him.

Hardin didn't pull over until he was on a bridge with no exits. By the time Marty arrived, four town police cars and a state trooper were already gathered behind Hardin, lights flashing. Martin waved to Sergeant Cox, who came over to his window.

"He just lost his brakes," Marty said. "He doesn't even slow down."

Cox nodded.

Marty happened to know that the inspection from the month before had been clean, and he knew that Hardin hadn't reported a problem.

One of the rookie officers led Hardin, dazed and wide-eyed, back to a cruiser and sat him down in the backseat. Cox came back to Marty.

"We're going to impound the cab," Cox said. "The mechanic says there's no way he could have lost his brakes unless somebody cut the line."

"How would he know?"

"Under state law he's got to report any defect within two hours."

Marty watched as they put the safety edit on Hardin's cab and hooked it up to a flatbed.

"You think maybe some joker squirting brake fluid all over the highway?" Cox asked.

"It's what I'd think if he was the only one in trouble."

Cox nodded.

Pete was waiting anxiously when Marty got back to the garage.

"What happened?" he asked.

"Hardin. No brakes. They're impounding the cab."

Pete shook his head.

"That's bad. We're short one car."

The traffic light was out on Millport Road, and a pickup had pulled around a car stopped at the intersection. Marty pulled into the crosswalk and waited his turn. A dog with a limp darted past the front of his hood, then doubled back. In the rearview mirror Marty saw the reflection of the headlights coming up behind him, too close for the intersection, already turning.

A hundredth customer. One ride too late.

The web page started showing some of the history of the Route 9 numbers. Each month was divided into days, with the total number of rides for that day on the chart. So Marty started adding up the days for March: 89 plus 112, plus 78…

When he finished, he looked at the result. It wasn't nine thousand and thirty-two. It was eight thousand four hundred and eighteen.

And he knew why.

Old Man Hemlock.

Hemlock was ninety-three, blind, and kept to himself. He took the Route 9 bus twice a day, every day, to the diner.

Marty had watched him at work himself a dozen times. Hemlock would stand at the bus stop, take a step onto the bus, and announce, "One."

Then he'd sit in the same seat, and when he got to the diner, he'd announce, "One."

Marty was sure he'd seen the driver, a young woman with bright pink hair, count each "One" as being two passengers.

And sure enough, there it was: in February, when the numbers started to lag, the bus driver's runs had suddenly leaped up by an average of fifteen passengers a day.

Marty sat there for a long time after that. He didn't know what he should do.

The bus service had committed to a route it didn't earn, a route that meant he and Pete were going to have a harder time. He knew it was wrong, but telling the truth would mean exposing a diligent, but perhaps clueless, driver, and penalizing a very old man who just wanted a sandwich.

He turned the phone off and began to drive. He had a fare to pick up, a woman to take to physical therapy, and a younger generation to leave a future to.

Maybe some things were better left buried.

The old man, who asked for nothing, who just sat on the Route 9 playing the numbers game, was counting on that.

Marty read the report. The final week had been the best, with an average of one hundred fifty rides a day. What that meant was, something had changed.

He drove the neighborhood to see if he could find out what. A few of his usual passengers rode the bus now, but they said it was convenient. Then his wife called on the radio.

"Old Man Hemlock just called," she said. "Wants a ride to the library. Says he heard something on the radio this morning."

Old Man Hemlock lived on the hill, one of the farthest points on Marty's route. When Marty picked him up, Hemlock was already holding a newspaper.

"Heard on the radio this morning," Hemlock said. "That the bus driver, young man named Kevin, he had a heart attack at the library yesterday."

"Heart attack?" Marty said. "Is he... okay?"

"Report said he'll make a full recovery. But they canceled the bus for a week while they find somebody to train. They're saying it might be two weeks before the route is fully running again." Hemlock tapped the newspaper. "That's why everybody's using cabs again."

Marty looked at Hemlock, then out the window. He’d been so focused on the numbers, he hadn't even thought to ask what was happening with the driver. It wasn’t the route itself that had saved it. It was a person: Kevin, the bus driver, who now needed the town to ride with him, just to get back on the road.

He drove Old Man Hemlock to the library and checked his phone again. There were three calls waiting. He sighed, a weary, knowing sigh. 

"Busy day," he said to himself.


This story explores themes of unintended consequences, the importance of human connection, and small-town life. In response to international efforts to reduce deaths from road crashes – for example, the Decade of Action for Road Safety 2011-2020 – scores of countries have made serious efforts to address road safety. Although important lessons have been learned about what works to reduce road crash deaths, special attention needs to be given to vulnerable road users, such as motorcyclists and pedestrians. New approaches are required to rethink the design of the road transport system, using a holistic and integrated approach that applies a road safety perspective along the entire decision chain from planning of the transport system, infrastructure, vehicles and operation – not only their independent contributions, but also their interaction. Such an approach is essential if the ambitious international road safety targets are to be reached, for example ‘a 50 per cent global reduction in road fatalities by 2020'*.

Road fatalities are not accidental; they are a direct consequence of the way infrastructure, vehicles and road users are managed together in speed space. Decisions made separately across the chain impact road safety and performance of each building block in isolation. The interdependency of the road transport system components is not fully assessed in the present decision-making processes.
It is clear that the existing separate decision-making processes for the three main building blocks of the road transport system – road users, road infrastructure and vehicles - impede the identification of potential conflicts between these elements, thus resulting in poor roadway design and decision-making. These factors, separately or in combination, make all modes of road transport vulnerable to crashes, including vulnerable road users such as motorcyclists and pedestrians. A simple numerical example can serve to illustrate this.

Suppose a 20 per cent speed increase causes a 100 per cent increase in pedestrian fatalities (SFIF). In order to achieve the same fatality levels, the infrastructure would need to be modified to provide vehicles with an Absolute Braking Distance (ABD) of 120 per cent of the current distance.

This would be difficult to achieve as the measurements are taken with the brakes fully locked, thus overestimating the distance required, making 120 per cent a particularly challenging target. "I'll kill myself": so goes the familiar refrain, whenever anyone feels their life falling apart after something unexpected. This could be getting fired from a job, being diagnosed with a serious illness, failing a big exam, or going through any other major setback. Usually, this goes along with some variation on "things will not get better."

Nowhere is this "permanent emotional setback" more common than in divorce. People drive themselves crazy imagining they'll never recover, they'll never have a relationship again, or they'll never recover the wealth they used to have. They often feel empty and lost. Yet the divorce rate in the United States is about forty percent, which means that any person has an incredibly high probability of going through a divorce and re-adjusting to it. The majority of people come out of divorce with their financial and emotional health intact.

Adults spend all their lives adjusting to major changes. We fail at some things and succeed at others. We build careers (maybe even multiple ones), have kids, and go through every other life stage. Emotions are a constant state of flux -- you probably don't feel happy all the time, and you experience sadness, anger, and disappointment on a non-regular, but steady basis. That's just part of the human condition, and it's nothing to be ashamed of.

What's funny about this is that a kid of any age -- a toddler, a teenager, or maybe even a twenty week old -- can't usually have this type of all-encompassing emotional meltdown. Saying "it's been like this for thirteen of my seventeen years" isn't relevant to the shrink because it's not helpful to anyone. We should apply this same reality check to ourselves. Immature emotions never really work.

It's the emotional captive curling up in the fetal position; what everyone needs to do is just get up and start walking again.

You just got divorced? You failed at your new business venture? You were fired from your great job? So what?!
